name: Mangan
tagline: District headquarters above the Teesta, gateway to Dzongu
meta_description: Mangan, HQ of Mangan district (North Sikkim): banks, Dzongu permits, cardamom country and the halfway stop to Lachung and Lachen. Costs and tips for 2026.
summary: Mangan is the headquarters of Mangan district (North Sikkim), a small hill town about 67 km and 2.5–3 hours north of Gangtok on the North Sikkim Highway. Travellers use it as the lunch stop on the way to Lachung and Lachen, the place to get a Dzongu permit, and the last town with banks and pharmacies.
intro: Mangan sits on a ridge above the east bank of the Teesta, looking straight across the gorge to the forested slopes of Dzongu. Wikipedia gives its average elevation as 956 m, though the town climbs well above that along the highway. It is not a resort town. It is the working capital of Sikkim's largest district: government offices, the district hospital, schools, a market, a few banks and a line of small hotels and eating places where North Sikkim tour jeeps stop for lunch.

For most visitors Mangan passes in forty minutes over a plate of rice and dal. It deserves a little more if you are going to Dzongu, because the district administration here issues the Dzongu permit, and Lepcha homestay hosts often pick guests up in the bazaar. It is also a sensible halfway night when you start late from Bagdogra, or when a landslide above Toong holds up traffic. Singhik, 4 km up the road, has one of the best views of the Kangchenjunga range in the district.

Mangan district is cardamom country. Large cardamom, the smoky black spice used in garam masala, grows in the shade of alder trees on the slopes all around, and Mangan is a trading point for the crop. At this height the climate is mild: warm and humid in the monsoon, cool and clear from October to March. No protected area permit is needed for the town itself, but everything beyond the Toong check post, and Dzongu across the river, needs one. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: Where Namsoong comes to the riverbank
story.text: Mangan is the town nearest to Namprikdang, a riverside ground on the Teesta at the edge of Dzongu that has become the best known public venue for Namsoong, the Lepcha new year. Namsoong falls around December and January by the Lepcha calendar, and since 1979, according to the festival notes we use for our own Namsoong page, Lepcha organisations have gathered at Namprikdang for prayers by Bongthing and Mun priests, archery, traditional games, dances and Lepcha food. The setting matters. Across the river from Mangan lies Dzongu, the reserve that a Chogyal-era proclamation set aside for the Lepcha, and the Lepcha people are generally considered the earliest inhabitants of Sikkim, as the Wikipedia article on the Lepcha people records. Mangan district has more Lepcha speakers than any other district in Sikkim: the 2011 census found that 31.7 percent of its people named Lepcha as their first language. If you visit at the turn of the year, ask us whether the gathering is open to visitors that year, follow your hosts' lead, and ask before you photograph anyone.
story.source: Wikipedia, Lepcha people and Mangan district (Census of India 2011); Sikkim Escapes festival notes on Namsoong

little_known.fact: Mangan district is the largest of Sikkim's six districts by area, according to Wikipedia, yet its headquarters town had a population of only 4,644 at the 2011 census.
Until December 2021 the district was called North Sikkim; it was renamed Mangan district after its headquarters when Sikkim reorganised from four districts to six.
In the 2011 census Lepcha was the most common first language in the district at 31.7 percent, ahead of Nepali at 23.2 percent.
little_known.source: Census of India 2011, via Wikipedia, Mangan district

facts: District HQ, Dzongu permits, cardamom, lunch stop
Not needed for Mangan; needed for Dzongu and beyond Toong

highlights.title: The view across to Dzongu
highlights.text: From the highway and the viewpoint above the bazaar you look straight across the Teesta gorge to Dzongu's terraced villages, cardamom forest and waterfalls. On a clear morning snow peaks rise at the head of the valley. It is the best way to understand why Dzongu feels apart: a deep river and a single road separate it.

highlights.title: Dzongu permit and pickup point
highlights.text: The district administration in Mangan issues the permit for Dzongu, usually on weekdays and in the first half of the day. Most homestays apply on your behalf if you send ID in advance, and many hosts collect guests in Mangan bazaar. Check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Lunch on the North Sikkim run
highlights.text: Shared and private jeeps to Lachung and Lachen usually stop in or near Mangan for lunch: rice, dal, vegetables, eggs or chicken and noodle soups at simple roadside places. Pay at your own cost unless your package says otherwise, and do not linger too long, because the Toong check post closes to tourist vehicles at 4:00 pm.

highlights.title: Cardamom country
highlights.text: Large cardamom grows under shade trees across the district. From roughly September to November the pods are harvested and dried over wood fires in simple kilns, and sacks move through Mangan to traders. Ask a homestay host in Dzongu to show you a drying kiln if one is working.

highlights.title: Last town for cash and medicines
highlights.text: Mangan has bank branches, ATMs, pharmacies and the district hospital. Beyond it, Chungthang has an army medical centre and Lachung an SBI ATM that often runs dry. Draw cash and buy any medicines you need here or in Gangtok.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps to Mangan leave from the North Sikkim taxi stand at Vajra in Gangtok through the morning, about 2.5–3 hours, for around ₹250–350 a seat. They fill up early, so be at the stand by 8 am. Check current status before you travel.
A reserved small car or SUV from Gangtok takes 2.5–3 hours for about 67 km via Kabi, the Seven Sisters Waterfall and Phodong. Expect about ₹3,500–5,000 one way. No permit is needed for Mangan itself.

Mangan is about 175–180 km from NJP or Bagdogra, 6–7 hours via Gangtok on NH10. When NH10 is closed by slides, drivers use the Kalimpong or Algarah roads, which add time. Most travellers break the journey in Gangtok.

costs: Small fee or free; check with your host
where_to_stay: Mangan has a handful of hotels along the highway and in the bazaar, mostly simple rooms used by government visitors and drivers. Hotel Tamarind on the highway is the larger option we use for a halfway night or a Dzongu day trip, with spacious rooms and views over the gorge, though upkeep is uneven. Budget lodges in the bazaar charge about ₹1,500–2,500 a room. For a more memorable night, cross the river and stay with a Lepcha family in Dzongu, 30–60 minutes away, which needs a permit.
tips: Draw cash in Mangan; there are no ATMs inside Dzongu and Lachung's ATM often runs dry.
If you are applying for a Dzongu permit in person, reach Mangan before noon on a weekday.
Keep lunch short on the way north: tourist vehicles must pass the Toong check post by 4:00 pm.
Carry a light rain jacket from May to September, when afternoon showers are common.
Mangan is a working town, so ask before photographing people, offices or the market.

experiences.title: Cardamom country around Mangan
experiences.cost: ≈ ₹1,500–2,500 for a local car; host visit by arrangement
experiences.summary: Learn how large cardamom, Sikkim's best known spice, is grown under shade trees and dried over wood fires in the slopes around Mangan and Dzongu. Best during the autumn harvest, when kilns are working and the smoke smells of spice.
body: Large cardamom, also called black cardamom, is the smoky spice that goes into garam masala and many meat dishes across India. It grows in Sikkim as a shrub in the understorey of shaded forest, often under Himalayan alder, and the slopes of Mangan district, including Dzongu across the river, are among the places where it is most widely farmed. The plants flower in spring and the red pods cluster at the base of the stems close to the ground.

The harvest runs roughly from September to November. Families cut the pod clusters, separate them and dry them in a bhatti, a simple kiln where the pods sit on a rack over a wood fire for a day or more. That smoke is where the flavour comes from. The dried pods are packed into sacks and sold to traders who carry them down the highway through Mangan and Singtam.

This is not a formal tour. We arrange it through a host family, usually in Dzongu or a village near Mangan, who are happy to show their fields and kiln when work allows. Prices for cardamom swing sharply from year to year and disease has hit many growers, so ask about that too. Buy a small bag directly from the family if they offer it.

faqs.q: When is cardamom harvested in North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Large cardamom in Sikkim is usually harvested from about September to November, depending on altitude and the year. Lower fields are picked first. During these weeks drying kilns work day and night, and the smell of wood smoke and spice carries across the slopes. Outside the season you can still see the plants, but not the drying.

faqs.q: Can I buy cardamom directly from farmers in Mangan?
faqs.a: Sometimes, if the family you visit has dried pods to spare and offers them. Prices follow the market and change a lot between years, so do not haggle hard. You can also buy packed cardamom in Mangan and Gangtok shops. Carry it in a sealed bag, since the smoky smell spreads through luggage.

faqs.q: Is large cardamom the same as green cardamom?
faqs.a: No. Large or black cardamom, Amomum subulatum, is a different plant from the small green cardamom of South India. Its pods are bigger, darker and dried over fire, which gives them a smoky taste suited to rich curries and rice dishes. Sikkim has long been one of the main producing regions.

experiences.title: A slow stop in Mangan bazaar
experiences.summary: Use your Mangan stop well: collect a Dzongu permit, draw cash, buy local produce and eat lunch in the bazaar of the district headquarters. An hour here shows everyday North Sikkim life that tour jeeps usually rush past.
body: Mangan's bazaar runs along the highway and the lanes just above it: grocery shops, pharmacies, bank branches, small hardware stores and eating houses that serve rice meals, momos and thukpa. Government staff, farmers coming in from the villages and drivers on the North Sikkim run all pass through. It is the place where people from Dzongu, Singhik and the villages around come to shop and do business.

If you are heading to Dzongu, this is where the permit is issued by the district administration. Your homestay can usually apply in advance with copies of your ID and photos; if not, aim to reach Mangan on a weekday morning. While the paperwork moves, draw cash, buy fruit and snacks, and pick up any medicines you might need for the days ahead.

On the way to Lachung or Lachen, Mangan is the usual lunch stop. Ask your driver for a place that cooks fresh, and look out for local greens and seasonal vegetables. Keep an eye on the clock: the Toong check post shuts to tourist vehicles at 4:00 pm. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do I get the Dzongu permit?
faqs.a: The Dzongu permit is issued by the district administration in Mangan. Most Lepcha homestays apply for guests in advance if you send ID copies and photos a few days ahead, and that is the easiest way. If you apply in person, go on a weekday and reach Mangan before noon. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs in Mangan?
faqs.a: Yes. Mangan has branches and ATMs of several banks, which makes it the last reliable place for cash on the North Sikkim Highway. Dzongu has no ATMs, and the SBI ATM in Lachung often runs out in peak season. Draw enough for homestays, tips and add-ons before going further.

faqs.q: How long is the lunch stop at Mangan?
faqs.a: On a North Sikkim tour, the lunch stop around Mangan is usually 30–45 minutes. Drivers keep it short because tourist vehicles must cross the Toong check post by 4:00 pm. If you want more time in Mangan, plan a private car or a night here instead of squeezing it into the drive day.

experiences.title: Down to the Teesta at Namprikdang
experiences.summary: Drive down from Mangan to the Teesta at Namprikdang, the riverside ground where the Lepcha new year gathering is held, and see the river that carved North Sikkim. Best on a clear winter morning, with care near the water.
body: The Teesta rises in the glaciers of northern Sikkim and runs the length of the state before leaving for the plains. Below Mangan it flows in a deep gorge, and the road down to the river and the bridges into Dzongu drops steeply through cardamom and forest. Namprikdang is a flat ground near the confluence area on the Dzongu side, best known as the venue for the Namsoong celebrations of the Lepcha new year.

Outside festival days it is a quiet place to stand by the river and look back up at Mangan on its ridge. The October 2023 flood from South Lhonak Lake and later monsoon slides changed the riverbed and damaged roads and bridges along this stretch, so the banks today are rougher than in older photographs. Stay well away from the water's edge, which can rise without warning when dams upstream release water.

Ask your driver about current road conditions before going down. Access to some riverside points may need the Dzongu permit, depending on where you stop. Combine the drive with a homestay pickup or a short visit to Singhik for the view from above.

faqs.q: What is Namprikdang?
faqs.a: Namprikdang is a riverside ground on the Teesta at the edge of Dzongu, below Mangan. It is best known as the venue for the public Namsoong celebrations of the Lepcha new year around December and January, with prayers, archery, games and dances. On other days it is a quiet spot by the river.

faqs.q: Is it safe to go near the Teesta below Mangan?
faqs.a: Stay on the bank and keep well back from the water. The river is fast and cold, its course changed after the 2023 flood, and levels can rise suddenly. Do not swim, wade or climb on boulders for photographs. In the monsoon we do not recommend going down at all.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Namprikdang?
faqs.a: Namprikdang lies at the edge of Dzongu, and rules depend on exactly where you go. For a festival visit or a drive into Dzongu proper, carry a Dzongu permit issued in Mangan. Ask us or your host before you go, and check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: A halfway night on the way north
experiences.best_time: Any open month, especially after a late start
experiences.summary: Break the long North Sikkim drive with a night in Mangan. It eases the climb to Lachung or Lachen, avoids a rush to the Toong check post and leaves time for Singhik and the Naga Waterfall. Useful for families, seniors and late arrivals.
body: Most North Sikkim trips go from Gangtok to Lachung or Lachen in one long day of 5–7 hours. That works for many people, but not for everyone. If you land at Bagdogra in the afternoon, are travelling with older parents, or simply hate long days in a jeep, a night in Mangan at about 1,000 m splits the journey and means you never race the 4:00 pm cut-off at Toong.

The next morning you can stop at Singhik for the Kangchenjunga view, at the Naga Waterfall before Toong, and at Chungthang where the rivers meet, and still reach Lachung or Lachen by early afternoon. Your registered agent must plan the permit dates around the extra night, so tell us at the booking stage. Check current status before you travel.

Mangan's hotels are simple. Hotel Tamarind is the larger option; smaller lodges in the bazaar cost less. The town has a hospital, pharmacies and banks, which gives some peace of mind on a first day north. Sleep early: North Sikkim mornings start early.

faqs.q: Is it worth staying a night in Mangan?
faqs.a: It is worth it if you arrive in Gangtok late, travel with seniors or young children over five, or want to visit Dzongu or Singhik. It turns one long drive into two shorter ones and removes the pressure of the Toong 4:00 pm cut-off. For a quick 2N/3D trip most people drive straight through.

faqs.q: Does a Mangan night count towards the North Sikkim minimum stay?
faqs.a: Operators require a minimum of two nights in the protected areas of North Sikkim, which means Lachung, Lachen and beyond. Mangan lies below the Toong check post, so a night here is usually extra rather than part of that minimum. Ask us how it affects your permit dates.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Mangan?
faqs.a: Mangan is mild for most of the year. Winter days from December to February are cool and clear, around 8–18 °C, and nights get cold. Spring and autumn are pleasant. From June to September it is warm, humid and rainy, with landslides on the highway, so plan cautiously in the monsoon.

faqs.q: How far is Mangan from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Mangan is about 67 km from Gangtok on the North Sikkim Highway via Kabi and Phodong, which takes 2.5–3 hours by car in normal conditions. Shared jeeps leave from the Vajra taxi stand in Gangtok in the morning. Landslides can add hours in the monsoon, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Mangan?
faqs.a: No. Mangan town and the highway up to the Toong check post do not need a protected area permit for Indian travellers. You do need a separate permit for Dzongu across the river, and a protected area permit through a registered agent for Chungthang, Lachung, Lachen and beyond. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Mangan?
faqs.a: Wikipedia gives Mangan's average elevation as 956 m, and the town spreads uphill along the highway to around 1,200 m. Either way it is low enough that altitude is not a concern. It is a good place to start acclimatising before Lachung at about 2,700 m or Lachen at about 2,750 m.

faqs.q: Is Mangan the same as North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Mangan is the headquarters town of Mangan district, which until December 2021 was called North Sikkim district. Travellers and tour operators still say North Sikkim. The district covers Mangan, Dzongu, Chungthang, Lachung, Lachen, Thangu, Gurudongmar and the villages along the highway from Kabi northwards.

faqs.q: What is there to see in Mangan?
faqs.a: Mangan is a working town rather than a sightseeing stop. The main draws are the view across the Teesta to Dzongu, the bazaar, cardamom farms on the surrounding slopes, the Singhik viewpoint 4 km away, and the Naga Waterfall further up the highway. It is also the gateway for Dzongu permits.

faqs.q: Where can I stay in Mangan?
faqs.a: Hotel Tamarind on the highway is the larger hotel we use, with spacious rooms and views, though maintenance is uneven. Smaller lodges in the bazaar cost about ₹1,500–2,500 a room. For a more personal stay, cross to Dzongu and stay with a Lepcha family, which needs a permit.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Mangan?
faqs.a: Foreign nationals with the online Sikkim restricted area permit can travel the highway through Mangan. Rules for Dzongu and for areas beyond Toong are stricter: foreigners may visit Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point on a group permit with a registered agent. For Dzongu, ask us. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Mangan?
faqs.a: October to December brings clear skies and views of the snow peaks from Singhik, and March to May is warm and green. The monsoon, June to September, brings heavy rain and landslides on the highway. Around December and January the Lepcha Namsoong festival is celebrated at nearby Namprikdang.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and ATM in Mangan?
faqs.a: Yes. Mangan has mobile coverage from the main networks and several bank branches with ATMs, plus pharmacies and the district hospital. It is the last town on the highway with reliable services, so draw cash and buy essentials here before Dzongu, Lachung or Lachen.
